statement: Two players play a match. Every game has a winner, and the first player to win 2 games wins the match. How many different orders of game winners can a match have?

choices.misconception: I counted only who wins the match, not the different ways the games can go.
I listed the ways one player can win the match and forgot the other player.
I listed only the ways two games can turn out and forgot that a match can need a third game.
I listed all the results of three games, even when the match was already over after two.

hints: Draw a tree: the first game, then the second.
Make a tree diagram. Each game branches two ways, but a branch stops as soon as someone has 2 wins. Count the ends of the branches.
After two games: AA and BB end the match. AB and BA each need a third game, which can go either way.

solutions.reliable: Call the players A and B and draw a tree. If one player wins both of the first two games the match ends: AA or BB. If the first two games are split, AB or BA, a third game decides it, giving ABA, ABB, BAA and BAB. That is 2 + 4 = 6 orders. The transferable idea: in a tree diagram, stop a branch the moment the outcome is decided, otherwise you count games that are never played.

whyOnTest: Tree diagrams test whether you stop branches that are already finished instead of counting every possible sequence.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
